opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the answer has shifted a lot over the last year or so. My general mental model is that the large frontier models are where you get the capability you actually need for agentic work. When you're building an agent, you're asking the model to do a lot of things at once: plan over a long horizon, decide which tools to call, recover when something goes wrong, and keep track of a lot of context. Those are the capabilities that really scale with model size and with the kind of reinforcement learning the big labs are doing. So if you're starting a new agentic application, my strong advice is to start with the biggest, most capable model you can get your hands on. Figure out whether the task is even possible before you worry about cost or latency.

Where small models come in is once you understand the problem really well. If you've got a workflow that's narrow, repeatable, and you've collected a lot of data on what good behavior looks like, then you can often distill that down into a much smaller model, or fine-tune a small model on just that slice of the task. You get big wins on latency and cost, and sometimes even on reliability, because the model isn't trying to be good at everything.

So in practice I think a lot of the most interesting systems end up being hybrid. You have a big model doing the hard reasoning and orchestration, and then smaller, specialized models handling well-defined subtasks like classification, extraction, routing, or summarizing tool outputs. The mistake I see people make is going small too early. They optimize for cost before they've figured out whether the agent actually works, and they end up spending months fighting the model instead of learning about their problem. Get it working with the best model first, build up your evals and your data, and then use that to decide where a smaller model can safely take over.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's probably the most common question we get from teams building agents. And the honest answer is that it depends a lot on where you are in the lifecycle of the application.

When you're starting out, I think you should almost always reach for the biggest, most capable model you can get your hands on. The reason is that in the early phase, your problem isn't cost or latency, your problem is figuring out whether the thing can work at all. Agentic tasks are hard. You're chaining together many steps, you're calling tools, you're recovering from errors, and a small mistake early in the trajectory compounds. Large models are just dramatically better at that kind of long-horizon reasoning and at being robust to the weird edge cases you didn't anticipate in your prompt. So if you start with a small model and it fails, you don't actually learn much. You don't know if the task is impossible, if your scaffolding is wrong, or if the model is just too weak. Starting big removes one of those variables.

Where small models become really interesting is once you've actually gotten something working and you understand the shape of the problem. At that point, a few things are true. You've usually got a pile of real traces from the big model, so you have data. You've narrowed the task from "do anything an agent might do" to a much more specific distribution of inputs and tool calls. And you've started to feel the pain of cost and latency, because agents make a lot of calls per user interaction, so a model that's five or ten times cheaper and faster is a very big deal in practice.

And small models, when they're fine-tuned on a narrow task, can be extremely good. Often they'll match or beat the frontier model on the specific thing you care about, because you're trading away generality you don't need for reliability on the distribution you actually see. The caveat is that they're brittle. The moment the input drifts outside what they were trained on, they fall apart in ways a large model wouldn't, so you need good evals and good monitoring to know when that's happening.

So the pattern I like is to think of it less as small versus large and more as a routing problem inside the agent. There are usually a few steps that are genuinely hard, like planning, or recovering when something goes wrong, or handling an ambiguous user request, and those deserve the biggest model you can afford. Then there are a lot of steps that are pretty mechanical, like extracting structured data from a tool result, classifying intent, deciding which of three tools to call next, and those are great candidates for a small specialized model. If you decompose the agent that way, you get most of the quality of the big model at a fraction of the cost.

The last thing I'd say is that the line keeps moving. What counts as a "small" model today is more capable than the frontier model from a couple of years ago. So I'd be careful about baking in assumptions. Build your system so you can swap models easily, keep your evals tight, and re-run the experiment every few months, because the right answer genuinely changes over time.

r001.rationale: The response says models keep improving and recommends revisiting the choice, but it does not clearly state that the potential to improve small models remains unexhausted.

r002.rationale: It says large models handle unforeseen edge cases more robustly, while small models can fail when inputs drift beyond their training distribution, conveying a generalization advantage for unexpected cases.

astra-6.text:
I think about it less as small models versus large models and more as, what are you asking the model to do, and how much context does it need to do that reliably?

If you have a fairly narrow task, where you can define what success looks like and collect representative examples, a small model can be a really good fit. You can potentially get the quality you need with much lower latency and cost. And in an agentic application, those things compound because you might be making a lot of model calls to complete one user request.

The larger models are particularly useful when the task is open-ended—when the agent needs to handle an unfamiliar situation, reason across multiple sources of information, or recover when a tool call doesn't do what it expected. Those are harder behaviors to capture in a narrowly specialized model.

So my starting point would usually be to get the application working with a capable model and build an evaluation around the actual tasks users care about. Then you can ask, which parts can a smaller model handle? You might use one for routing or extracting information, and keep a larger model for the more difficult decisions. The important thing is to evaluate the whole workflow, because a cheaper individual call isn't necessarily cheaper overall if it causes the agent to make more attempts or fail more often.

r001.rationale: The response compares task fit and suggests using smaller models for narrow tasks, but does not say that the potential to improve small models remains unexhausted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to think about it is in terms of the task you're asking the model to do. For a narrow, well-defined task, a small model can be a really good fit. You can get lower latency and lower cost, and if you have good examples of the behavior you want, you can often customize it pretty effectively.

But agentic applications also involve situations where you don't know in advance exactly what the model is going to encounter. It has to interpret a request, decide which tools to use, and recover when something goes wrong. That's where the capabilities of a larger model can become really valuable.

So I wouldn't necessarily make that decision for the entire application. You might use a larger model for the parts that require more reasoning and a smaller model for a specific step in the workflow. The important thing is to have evaluations that reflect your actual use case, so you can tell whether that smaller model is doing the job reliably. Then you can make the cost and latency tradeoffs based on evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says small models can be customized effectively with good examples, but does not say their improvement potential remains unexhausted.
